Note · Sandel — Justice

4 min read937 wordsUpdated 2026-06-06notes/canon/canon-sandel-justice.md

Canon · Cluster: Ethics & Judgment · Maps to Course 11 (Global Strategy & Responsible Business), E4 (Governance & The Board)

  • Source: Michael Sandel, Justice: What's the Right Thing to Do? (2009)
  • Core claim: There are three major approaches to justice, each powerful and each with a blind spot — and the practical skill is recognizing which framework you're implicitly using, and when to shift.
  • Framework — the three lenses: 1. Maximizing welfare (utilitarianism) — the greatest good for the greatest number. Blind spot: can justify sacrificing the individual for aggregate benefit; reduces all values to one scale. 2. Respecting freedom (libertarianism / Kantian rights) — individual rights and consent above collective outcomes. Blind spot: can tolerate vast inequality so long as it arose from free exchange. 3. Cultivating virtue (communitarianism / Aristotelian) — what promotes human flourishing and the common good. Blind spot: whose definition of virtue prevails?
  • Most real arguments are people talking past each other from different lenses without naming them.
  • Applies when: ESG, governance, responsible-business tradeoffs, fairness debates, policy — any decision where "the right thing" is contested and stakeholders argue from different moral premises.
  • Breaks when: the survey diagnoses without deciding — it sharpens which framework you're using but refuses to adjudicate between them, so it can leave you articulate and still stuck (a sophisticated relativism). It's also deliberative and slow — useless in the fast, recognition-primed moment (canon klein sources of power); it's a tool for set-piece ethical reasoning. And utilitarian "maximize welfare" quietly underwrites a lot of business logic (cost-benefit, canon mankiw principles of economics) — worth seeing the lens you default to.
  • Practitioner counterpoint: (researched 2026-06-05 — r/Ethics corpus + Harvard "Justice" transcripts) The corpus is a live demonstration of Sandel's thesis: the most-upvoted r/Ethics threads are unacknowledged framework clashes, not disagreements about facts. A 1,144↑ post — "the debate around abortions shows how bad most people are at assessing and discussing ethical dilemmas" — diagnoses exactly this: "any debate around the topic is abysmal, with everyone just making oversimplified, politicized propaganda statements… almost no one seems to be able to admit that [it] is a very complex and difficult ethical dilemma." A 399↑ thread — "I hate the phrase 'There's no ethical consumption under capitalism'" — is a rights-vs-welfare collision dressed as a slogan, with the OP arguing ethics is "a spectrum of harm reduction" against an absolutist "all-or-nothing" frame. The usable move: name which lens each party is arguing from (welfare / rights / virtue) before arguing the case. Badaracco's right-vs-right is the personal-scale version (canon badaracco defining moments).
  • Researched layer (2026-06-05)
  • Canonical explanation (sourced): Sandel's whole course turns on a single distinction that maps onto two of the three lenses. From the opening trolley lecture: "consequentialist moral reasoning locates morality in the consequences of an act, in the state of the world that will result from the thing you do," whereas "categorical moral reasoning locates morality in certain absolute moral requirements, in certain categorical duties and rights, regardless of the consequences" (Harvard University, "The Moral Side of Murder"). The skill isn't picking one — it's noticing which one you're using when your intuition flips between cases.
  • Real application (mined): the trolley poll itself is the mechanism in miniature — the same person votes to divert the trolley (welfare: "better that five should live even if one must die") but refuses to push the fat man off the bridge (a categorical bar on using a person as a means). Sandel: "people weren't so sure about consequentialist moral reasoning when people hesitated to push the fat man over the bridge." The r/Ethics "eating dog vs. cow" thread (595↑) runs the same experiment on the reader — once culture is stripped out, people discover they were arguing from a virtue/tradition lens, not a welfare one.
  • Where the corpus pushes back on the book: Rawls' answer to the impasse — choose principles "behind the veil of ignorance," where you'd reject utilitarianism because "we will each want to be respected with dignity… even if we turn out to be a member of a minority" (Harvard, "What's a Fair Start?"). But the practitioner corpus shows the limit Sandel himself flags: naming the lenses sharpens the argument without ending it. The abortion thread's despair — "everyone is 100% sure that they are right" — is the lived version of the note's "diagnoses without deciding" critique. For operational ethics the corpus prefers a decision model: a Global Ethics Solutions transcript splits dilemmas into "situational" (judgment/temptation) vs. "not-so-situational," arguing the latter "require a decision-making model that allows you to clarify the situation and offer constructive alternatives" — structure Sandel deliberately withholds.
  • Sources in corpus: Harvard University — "Justice: Episode 01 'The Moral Side of Murder'" (youtube.com/watch?v=kBdfcR-8hEY) · "Episode 06 'Mind Your Motive'" (youtube.com/watch?v=8rv-4aUbZxQ) · "Episode 08 'What's a Fair Start?'" (youtube.com/watch?v=VcL66zx_6No) · Global Ethics Solutions — "Ethical Decision Making: Kinds of Ethical Dilemmas" (youtube.com/watch?v=x3lWS-M-WWY) · r/Ethics "the debate around abortions shows how bad most people are…" (1,144↑), "I hate the phrase 'There's no ethical consumption under capitalism'" (399↑), "Aside from culture why is eating dog worse than eating cow?" (595↑).

Rep

Take a contested "right thing to do" at work. State the case three ways — welfare, rights, virtue. Which lens are you defaulting to? Which one are the people who disagree with you using?

Marks itself read when you reach the end.
